value.body: After a B.Arch, some architects specialise rather than staying in general building design. Urban design deals with streets, public spaces and neighbourhoods; interior design deals with spaces inside buildings; BIM (Building Information Modelling) roles build and coordinate detailed digital models used by design and construction teams. Each can be entered through work experience, short courses or a master's.

items.label: Use of the title 'architect'
items.note: Registration with the Council of Architecture under the Architects Act, 1972

items.label: Interior design
items.note: Designers from other backgrounds also practise

value.title: How you get in
value.body: For urban design, a master's is the common route — admission through GATE (Architecture & Planning), CEED in some institutes, or university tests. For interiors, many architects move in through firm experience or a portfolio. BIM roles are usually entered by learning BIM software and coordination workflows, through courses or on the job.

value.title: At a glance
items: BIM skills are in demand in large firms, consultancies and international project teams, often in production-heavy roles.
Urban design work is mostly in consultancies and government or development-authority projects, with fewer openings.
Interior design work is plentiful but competitive, and income depends heavily on clients and portfolio.
A strong portfolio matters more than the specialisation's title.
